title: Dual Defense: Enhancing Privacy and Mitigating Poisoning Attacks in Federated Learning

C-a.quote: clipping operation before the next training round. This enhancement is designed to counteract more sophisticated model poisoning attacks that conventional similarity-based methods [29, 38] fail to address, as will be shown in the experiments section.
C-a.locator: §3.2; PURPOSE QUOTATIONS FOR EVERY COMPONENT, as non-negotiable 12 requires of this paper's privacy class. (1) The two-phase anomaly detection's purpose is resisting poisoned updates: "To effectively detect malicious models in encrypted updates, we propose a novel two-phase anomaly detection mechanism" (§1). (2) The clipping stage's purpose is the quotation above, and it is stated as covering what the detection stage cannot. (3) THE FHE STAGE IS EXCLUDED FROM THE COUNT under Amendment 3, because its stated purpose is privacy and not resisting poisoned updates: "DDFed initially leverages cutting-edge fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) to securely aggregate model updates, without the impractical requirement for non-colluding two-server setups and ensures strong privacy protection" (§1). C-a therefore reaches two on the detection stage and the clipping stage, with FHE contributing nothing to the code

C-b.quote: This enhancement is designed to counteract more sophisticated model poisoning attacks that conventional similarity-based methods [29, 38] fail to address, as will be shown in the experiments section.

coder_note:
THIS ROW OVERTURNS AN ASSUMPTION I HAD BEEN CARRYING ABOUT THE PRIVACY CLASS, AND A5 MUST STATE THE CORRECTION. Amendment 3 was written to stop privacy and compression components from inflating C-a, and the 22-row privacy class was expected to code C-a = NO in bulk for that reason. DDFed shows the amendment does not work that way: it excludes the PRIVACY COMPONENT, not the PAPER. FHE contributes nothing to this row's C-a, and the code still reaches YES, because the paper independently composes TWO defenses -- a two-phase anomaly detector and a clipping stage -- and states a poisoning-resistance purpose for each. The correct summary of Amendment 3's effect is therefore that it removes a component from the count, and whether the paper survives at C-a = YES depends on what else it composes. A5 must not claim the amendment suppresses the privacy class.

C-b IS THE STRONGEST FORM OF THE CRITERION AND IT IS THE SAME SENTENCE AS C-a's. "designed to counteract more sophisticated model poisoning attacks that conventional similarity-based methods fail to address" names the first constituent's family, names the attack region it fails on, and gives that as the reason for adding the second constituent. That is complementary threat coverage stated as a reason, not a pairing reported as a fact, which is exactly what C-b's operative clause demands.

C-d = YES, AND THE SUBTLETY IS WORTH RECORDING BECAUSE IT IS NEW TO THE FRAME. The stage that gets varied is the DP perturbation -- a privacy component, which Amendment 3 correctly refuses to count as a defense for C-a purposes. C-d's frozen text asks only that "the paper varies the upstream stage while holding the downstream mechanism and the attack fixed", and says nothing requiring the upstream stage to be a defense. It should not: the whole point of the identifying contrast is to learn what a mechanism does as a function of what reaches it, and a privacy-noise sweep read off the DETECTOR'S OWN effectiveness is precisely that measurement. So a component can be excluded from C-a and still serve as the varied upstream for C-d, and this is the first paper where the two codes turn on the same component in opposite ways. Rule 4's benefit of the doubt is not needed; the reading is direct.

This is also the frame's best example of a paper reading its contrast off the DOWNSTREAM MECHANISM rather than off the composed system. Most C-d = YES rows here report the composition's accuracy or ASR at each setting of the upstream knob; DDFed reports whether the detector still works. That is the stronger form of the contrast and closer to what Prop. prop:identification_full specifies.
